title: Sound and Fury Politics
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/david-austin-walsh
text:
Reviewed:
Hyperpolitics: Extreme Politicization Without Political Consequences
Anton Jäger
London, England: Verso, 2026.

 

Hyperpolitics is an odd book, right down to its cover. A plain lemon-yellow background with the title in all-caps, looking more like a heading on a term paper than the title on a book jacket. The eye is drawn to a full-color print of German photographer Wolfgang Tillmans’s enigmatic Love (Hands in Hair), a picture of a young woman dancing at a nightclub in 1989 with a fellow dancer caressing her hair. Were Hyperpolitics by any other author, one might be tempted to read the haunting image as an exercise in nostalgia for a time when it seemed possible to “dance away industry, politics, history itself.” But Anton Jäger is not a nostalgist—at least not for the heady days of the End of History. The thirty-two-year-old Belgian political theorist’s career has been driven by disenchantment with the world that 1989 hath wrought. And if Hyperpolitics does not present any definitive answers about what the Western left should do in the context of our contemporary political crisis, Jäger at least offers a convincing—if at times vague—structural explanation for how we got here.

Derived from a series of essays published in a variety of left-wing magazines and originally published in German in 2023, Hyperpolitics is less a work of bold new political thought than a clever reworking of various strains of Marxian-flavored political theory. Jäger offers a sketch, albeit a provocative one, presenting the political development of the last  hundred-odd years in four stages. The first, “mass politics,” was characterized by the dense civic associationalism of early-to-mid-twentieth-century industrial capitalism; it was followed by “postpolitics,” which roughly correlates with Robert Putnam’s thesis in his 2000 book Bowling Alone about the alienating effects of neoliberalism and the market revolution and the erosion of the political. The post-2008 populist turn brought “antipolitics” to the fore, only to give way to contemporary “hyperpolitics” characterized by intense repoliticization of everyday life, though without the dense associational structures of a century ago. Hyperpolitics, in Jäger’s sense, is simultaneously totalizing—both a reaction and contributor to the Sturm und Drang of the attention economy—and detached. He emphasizes repeatedly throughout the book that hyperpolitics is driven by, or at least commensurate with, market logic. Hyperpolitical actors, not rooted in specific institutions, organizations, or, indeed, self-reflexive political formations, always have the option to exit or withdraw from the market. This means that hyperpolitics is not, by definition, totalizing. The ability to exit the market lowers the stakes of political struggle. 

So far, so good, and the great strength of hyperpolitics as a concept is that it can be used to answer the question that Vincent Bevins, among others, has posed: Why did a decade of sustained political unrest—Occupy, Black Lives Matter, and the #MeToo movement—accomplish shockingly little in terms of concrete political changes? But Jäger’s obvious nostalgia for the totalizing age of mass politics at times undermines the analytical clarity of his argument. Even at the height of the age of mass politics in the 1920s and 1930s, most citizens—at least most middle-class citizens—in the West still had the choice to opt out of formal political struggle and retreat to private life. This was certainly true in the liberal democracies of the West and, to a far lesser extent, even in the fascist dictatorships. Scores of political opponents of the Nazi regime in Germany did not choose exile, go underground, or accept defeat and join the Nazi Party. They simply ceased to act politically. 

Jäger, to his credit, is sensitive at times to the sweeping nature of his claims. At one point, he acknowledges that conservative social institutions such as churches have weathered the decline of voluntary associations much more robustly than their counterparts on the left. But the nuances are important. Absent what Fredric Jameson called a “conception of the social totality”—that is, a completely totalizing form of political thought and organization dedicated to the complete transformation of the governing logic of profit and capital accumulation—one can always opt out of voluntary organizations, the political clubs, trade unions, affinity, or interest groups that form social life. 

There have, of course, been societies in the history of the twentieth century in which opting out was not possible, but Stalinist Soviet Union, Maoist China at the height of the Cultural Revolution, or Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge are rightly considered by the Westerm left to be cautionary tales on the dangers of authoritarianism and totalizing revolutionary fervor. Jäger, at least on some level, is aware of this, writing in his conclusion that his prescription of “drawing atomized individuals back into parties and unions may seem nostalgic, authoritarian, or simply unrealistic.” Certainly, the Western left was overeager to avoid the dangers of authoritarianism after Stalin,and particularly after the collapse of the Soviet Union, that wariness may have led contributed to the absence of strong leadership in the  revolts of Occupy and BLM in the 2010s. But the kind of sustained political mobilization without the option to opt out that Jaeger clearly envisions as necessary for meaningful political change requires sticks as well as carrots. Jäger is careful throughout to emphasize that hyperpolitics is not a specific political formation but the larger political foundation on which contemporary politics plays out. Nevertheless, hyperpolitics as he defines it—focused on short-term logics, “impermanent engagement,” and incorporating a “mode of viral panic typical of the Internet age with its short cycles of hype and outrage” without formal institutional structures—shares much with the interpretation of “wokeness” presented by American sociologist Musa al-Gharbi. 

To be sure, wokeness and hyperpolitics are not the same thing. Al-Gharbi defines “woke” as the governing ideology of contemporary elites. Borrowing from Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of symbolic capital, al-Gharbi argues that contemporary “symbolic capitalists”—which is to say the relatively small group that still aspires to upward mobility within the existing social, political, and economic power structures—embraced the language of “wokeness.” The term originated in the twentieth-century black radical tradition and was popularized among liberals and leftists in the 2010s to discuss and analyze real forms of systemic racism, sexism, and other forms of social discrimination. But, in practice, wokeness as a discourse in the 2010s often degenerated into the policing of individual behavior within elite spaces, ironically belying its radical roots. It conveyed an awareness of and a willingness to perform, in al-Gharbi’s words, “the appropriate scripts for cultural and intellectual elites in response to various cues.” 

In other words, the language of wokeness—ranging from antiracism and “allyship,” to social justice commitments more broadly—simultaneously represents real political commitments and a form of in-group signaling. Perhaps most strikingly, “woke” politics does not have an institutional basis beyond in-group cultural signaling. Conservatives often imagine a woke Central Committee enforcing party discipline, but there is no such thing. Insofar as “wokeness” has an institutional base, it is in the managerial strata of corporate structures, most notoriously the university. Al-Gharbi seems to suggest that wokeness is a totalizing force, at least within those spaces. One cannot aspire to a professorship, for instance, without at least minimal deployments of the language of wokeness to signal awareness and sensitivity. Yet wokeness as a politics remains in those spaces, and even there, it is structurally weak, as the ongoing purges of DEI programs and initiatives in American colleges and universities in the face of pressure from the Trump administration makes all too clear. In other words, the commitment of managerial elites to wokeness stemmed primarily from short-term political thinking.

All this is to say that wokeness is precisely the kind of political formation that one would expect to see emerge within the broader framework of hyperpolitics. It is no coincidence that its (fleeting) cultural power was the most tangible material consequence of the antipolitical protest decade. The most significant material consequence of social justice protest movements of the 2010s—the dismantling of Confederate memorials and other monuments to white supremacy—was simultaneously immensely culturally significant but also all but irrelevant to the more radical ambitions of police or prison abolitionists. And because of its cultural emphasis, woke remained, above all, primarily an elite-level phenomenon. It is little wonder that, especially as the most radical demands either burned out, abated, or were co-opted by a still-dominant neoliberalism, the terrain of the project shifted to representation and elite diversification as opposed to structural transformation. 

But the same could be said of wokeness’s primary political opponents on the MAGA Right, the loose network of intellectuals and organizations that Laura Field examines in her recent book Furious Minds. Her dramatis personae, ranging from academics such as Patrick Deneen to political and organizational entrepreneurs such as Michael Anton, are themselves almost universally elite intellectuals attempting to harness the social and political power of the right-wing populist turn to consolidate their own positions within the professional-managerial class. (Unlike their counterparts on the left, who at least initially had broader and more transformational political goals, the MAGA right was always a self-consciously elitist project.) Since the 2024 election, analysis from centrist and center-right writers like Thomas Chatterton Williams has taken on the so-called “woke right,” arguing that figures like Anton or Christopher Rufo are simply mirror images of the identitarian politics they profess to despise. This is directionally correct but misses the key point: Both the “woke” and their opponents on the right are responding to the incentives of the hyperpolitical age. 

Is there a way out of hyperpolitics? Jäger himself is maddeningly vague. He ends on a predictably pessimistic note on the inadequacy of intellectual diagnosis of a broader historical problem. But there is nevertheless room for cautious optimism that the left, at least, is beginning to grow out of the hyperpolitical trap. “Wokeness,” at least in its 2010s identitarian variety, no longer commands the political, cultural, and social capital it once did. This is partly an organic response to changing political circumstances—namely the failure of social justice activism to achieve its transformational political goals—as well as the result of a deliberate political project on the left. Jäger himself notes in his afterward that part of the inspiration for the book came from conversations with Bhaskar Sunkara, the founder of Jacobin magazine and currently the president of The Nation, who has long believed that the “left had something to learn from Robert Putnam.” These publications, as well as others such as New Left Review, not only emphasize the need for institution-building on the left but also criticize the identitarian turn in left politics at the heart of wokeness. Many, although not all, leftist elected officials in 2026 are taking cues from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and distancing themselves from “Woke 1.” And there have been real political consequences to these shifts. The success of the Democratic Socialists of America in building a powerful political organization capable of electing the mayor of New York on the basis of a multiethnic, cross-class coalition is an important development, as is—to a lesser extent—the electoral victories of democratic socialist candidates in the 2026 Democratic primaries. 

These developments are emphatically not the totalizing social and political shift that Jäger obviously wishes to see. But they are not nothing. They suggest, at the minimum, that the American left has learned that wokeness, as one manifestation of the hyperpolitical age, has serious limits in its ability to affect broader systemic change, and is slowly but surely moving beyond it. But it is still too early to sound the death knell for hyperpolitics.
